paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

nodes.text: What are the neural mechanisms involved in feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility evoked by social decisions under risk?
nodes.description: The study investigated how brain regions respond when participants make risky choices that affect both themselves and a partner, particularly when those choices lead to negative outcomes for the partner.
nodes.anchor: investigated the neural mechanisms involved in feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility evoked by social decisions

nodes.text: Participant happiness decreases more following low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant rather than the partner made the choice.
nodes.description: This behavioral effect fits an operational definition of interpersonal guilt, where being responsible for a suboptimal outcome for someone with whom one has a positive social bond induces a negative emotional response.
nodes.anchor: happiness decreases following low outcomes for the partner were larger when the participant rather than their partner had made the choice

nodes.text: Activation in the left anterior insula reflects the guilt effect observed in behavior.
nodes.description: The left anterior insula showed increased BOLD signal when participants experienced guilt for low outcomes affecting their partner, compared to similar outcomes resulting from the partner's choices.
nodes.anchor: This guilt effect was associated with BOLD signal increase in the left anterior insula

nodes.text: Connectivity between left anterior insula and right inferior frontal gyrus varies depending on choice type and experimental condition.
nodes.description: This suggests that the right IFG is sensitive to guilt-related information during social choices.
nodes.anchor: Connectivity between this region and the right inferior frontal gyrus varied depending on choice and experimental condition

nodes.text: A computational model differentiating between partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant versus partner choices best explains variations in momentary happiness.
nodes.description: The Responsibility model, which separately models partner reward prediction errors from participant and partner choices, fitted the happiness data better than simpler models.
nodes.anchor: the Responsibility and Responsibility Redux models explained the data best

nodes.text: A left superior temporal sulcus region tracks partner reward prediction errors that followed participant choices more than those following partner choices.
nodes.description: This suggests a critical role of the STS in monitoring the consequences of one's risky decisions on others.
nodes.anchor: one cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus region showed a higher response to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices

nodes.text: Participants showed similar risk preferences when making decisions affecting only themselves versus themselves and their partner.
nodes.description: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions in either study, with only a slight tendency toward higher risk aversion in the Social condition in Study 1.
nodes.anchor: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions

nodes.text: Precuneus, left temporo-parietal junction, and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex are more engaged when participants decide for both themselves and their partner rather than just for themselves.
nodes.description: These regions are classically associated with social cognition and feelings of guilt.
nodes.anchor: Deciding for both self and partner rather than just for oneself evoked increased activations in precuneus, left TPJ, and dmPFC

nodes.text: Whole-brain activation patterns during guilt resembled a published neurometric marker of guilt.
nodes.description: The dot products between individual responses and the guilt-related brain signature were overall positive, indicating similarity.
nodes.anchor: The dot products between individual responses and the GRBS varied between –40.1 and 36.7, but overall these values were positive

nodes.text: In Study 1, participant happiness decreased more following low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant chose (t(39) = -3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.56) compared to when the partner chose, when the participant received the high lottery outcome.
nodes.description: This effect was replicated when the participant received the low lottery outcome (t(39) = -3.39, p = 0.002, d = 0.54).
nodes.anchor: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery

nodes.text: In Study 2, participant happiness decreased more following low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant chose (t(43) = -2.68, p = 0.01, d = 0.4) compared to when the partner chose, when the participant received the high lottery outcome.
nodes.description: This effect was replicated when the participant received the low lottery outcome (t(43) = -3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.54).
nodes.anchor: The 'guilt effect' occurred whether the participant received the high lottery outcome

nodes.text: In Study 2, the left anterior insula showed higher activation to low lottery outcomes for the partner following participant choices compared to partner choices (peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, p = 0.024 corrected for left anterior insula).
nodes.description: This small cluster within the left anterior insula survived correction for multiple comparisons restricted to the anatomically defined left anterior insula.
nodes.anchor: We found a weak response in a small cluster within the left anterior insula

nodes.text: In Study 2, bilateral ventral striatum activation increased with the amount of expected certain rewards and expected values of chosen lotteries (left: pFWE = 0.002, T = 5.63, d = 0.75; right: pFWE = 0.005, T = 5.46, d = 0.70).
nodes.description: This replicates previous findings associating ventral striatum with reward processing.
nodes.anchor: activation in bilateral ventral striatum indeed increased with the amount of expected certain rewards and the expected values of chosen lotteries

nodes.text: In Study 2, a cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus showed higher response to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices (pFWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, 100 voxels, peak at MNI [-52 -32 0]).
nodes.description: This suggests that this region tracks a partner's unexpected outcomes less when they do not follow from the participant's decisions.
nodes.anchor: We found this effect in one cluster within the left STS

nodes.text: In Study 2, functional connectivity between left anterior insula and right inferior frontal gyrus was highest when participants made risky choices for themselves and safe choices for both players (pFWE = 0.020, T = 4.34, d = 0.80, 115 voxels, peak at MNI [46 16 22]).
nodes.description: This pattern suggests that information processed in the insula is relayed to the IFG during social decisions.
nodes.anchor: a cluster in the right IFG whose connectivity to the insula (the seed region) was highest when participants made Risky choices for themselves and Safe choices for both players

nodes.text: In Study 2, three clusters showed greater activation when participants chose for both themselves and their partner rather than just for themselves: precuneus (d = 0.79), left temporo-parietal junction (d = 0.59), and medial prefrontal cortex (d = 0.54).
nodes.description: These regions are classically associated with social cognition.
nodes.anchor: Three significant clusters of voxels were identified, in the precuneus, the left temporo-parietal junction (TPJ) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)

nodes.text: In Study 2, bilateral ventral striatum showed greater response when participants chose the risky rather than the safe option (Cohen's d = 0.72 and 0.85 in left and right clusters, respectively).
nodes.description: This replicates previous findings associating ventral striatum with risky choice.
nodes.anchor: We searched for brain regions engaged more when participants chose the risky instead of the safe option and found such responses in the bilateral ventral striatum

nodes.text: In both studies, the Responsibility model fitted happiness data better than all other models including the Basic, Inequality, and Guilt-envy models (Study 1: all LR ≥47.36, p < 0.0001; Study 2: all LR ≥77.83, p < 0.0001).
nodes.description: The Responsibility model separately modeled partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant and partner choices.
nodes.anchor: a likelihood ratio test revealed that the Responsibility model fitted better than all the other models

nodes.text: In both studies, weights for partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant choices (social_pRPE) were greater than zero (Responsibility model: Study 1: Z = 2.85, p = 0.004; Study 2: Z = 3.26, p = 0.001).
nodes.description: This indicates that partner reward prediction errors for which participants were responsible contributed to explaining variations in happiness.
nodes.anchor: weights for social_pRPE were greater than 0

nodes.text: In Study 1, participants chose the risky option more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition (t(4796) = 2.54, p = 0.011, β = 0.164).
nodes.description: This difference was not found in Study 2.
nodes.anchor: Participants chose the lottery more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition in Study 1

nodes.text: In Study 2, the dot products between individual brain responses and the guilt-related brain signature were overall positive (mean = 5.22, median = 6.97, sign test: p = 0.017, Cliff's Delta = 0.4).
nodes.description: This indicates similarity between the activation patterns in this study and a published neurometric marker of guilt.
nodes.anchor: overall these values were positive (mean = 5.22; median = 6.97; sign test: p = 0.017

nodes.text: Study 1: Behavioral experiment with 40 participants performing risky choice task outside fMRI scanner
nodes.description: Participants repeatedly chose between safe and risky monetary outcomes in three conditions (Social, Partner, Solo) and reported momentary happiness every two trials. The experiment included three sessions.
nodes.anchor: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

nodes.text: Study 2: fMRI experiment with 44 participants performing risky choice task during fMRI scanning
nodes.description: Participants performed two sessions of the same risky choice task as Study 1 inside the fMRI scanner, with adjusted inter-stimulus intervals (3-11 s). BOLD responses were measured during decision-making and outcome phases.
nodes.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study)

nodes.text: Computational modeling analysis of happiness data from Studies 1 and 2
nodes.description: Five computational models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, Responsibility Redux) were fitted to momentary happiness ratings to assess influences of rewards, expected values, reward prediction errors, and inequality on happiness variations.
nodes.anchor: we fitted computational models to each participant's happiness data

nodes.text: fMRI region-of-interest analysis of decision-phase activation in Study 2
nodes.description: Linear mixed models were applied to BOLD parameter estimates from regions identified in contrasts (ventral striatum, precuneus, TPJ, mPFC) to assess how activation varied with choice type and experimental condition.
nodes.anchor: we analysed the responses in all the voxels in these regions using LMMs

nodes.text: fMRI region-of-interest analysis of outcome-phase activation in Study 2
nodes.description: Linear mixed models were applied to BOLD parameter estimates from regions responding to lottery outcomes (bilateral insula, dmPFC, STS, ventral striatum, dlPFC, parietal cortex) to identify regions involved in the guilt effect.
nodes.anchor: we analysed voxel responses using LMMs

nodes.text: Model-based fMRI analysis using computational model regressors in Study 2
nodes.description: BOLD responses were analyzed using regressors derived from the Responsibility computational model (certain rewards, expected values, participant and partner reward prediction errors) to identify brain regions tracking these variables.
nodes.anchor: We used the model to create expected BOLD responses for each participant

nodes.text: Psychophysiological interaction analysis of functional connectivity in Study 2
nodes.description: Seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses were performed using left anterior insula and left STS as seed regions to identify regions whose connectivity with these seeds varied as a function of choice type and experimental condition.
nodes.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses

nodes.text: Comparison of Study 2 activation patterns with published guilt-related brain signature
nodes.description: Individual brain responses to low partner outcomes following participant versus partner choices were compared to a multivariate guilt-related brain signature from Yu et al. 2020 using dot products.
nodes.anchor: we compared this brain signature to the neural responses obtained in our task

nodes.text: Risky choice task with three conditions: participants chose between safe and risky monetary options in Solo (affecting only participant), Social (participant chose for both), and Partner (partner chose for both) conditions, with lotteries played out independently for each player when risky option selected.
nodes.description: Trials included 20 mixed, 20 gain, and 20 loss trials per session. Safe and risky option positions were randomized. Participants had unlimited time to choose. Decisions were displayed for 2 s and lottery outcomes for 2.5 s. Inter-stimulus intervals were 1-2 s (Study 1) or 3-11 s (Study 2) drawn from gamma distributions.
nodes.anchor: participants were presented with pairs of monetary options (a safe and a risky option; the risky option was a lottery with equally probable high and low outcomes)

nodes.text: Momentary happiness assessment: every two trials, participants rated 'How happy are you right now?' on a continuous scale from 'very unhappy' to 'very happy' with 100 selectable options, starting cursor at midpoint.
nodes.description: Ratings were Z-scored for analysis to cancel out effects of different rating variabilities across participants.
nodes.anchor: Every two trials, one ISI after the outcome of the previous trial, participants were asked 'How happy are you right now?'

nodes.text: Ice-breaker game to create positive social bond: participants and partner took turns drawing half of a simple picture while blindfolded, following verbal instructions from their game partner, with encouragements and positive feedback throughout.
nodes.description: This 15-minute session created an agreeable social atmosphere and positive, non-competitive, sympathetic attitude between participants and partner.
nodes.anchor: participants played an ice breaker game with their experiment partner, in which both participant and partner took turns in drawing one half of a simple picture while being blindfolded

nodes.text: Mixed-effects logistic regression to model choices: dependent variable was choice of risky option (1=Yes, 0=No), explanatory variables were difference between expected value of lottery and safe option (EVdiff), condition (Solo=1, Social=2), and their interaction, with subject-specific random intercepts and slopes.
nodes.description: Model equation: Chose risky = F(β0 + (β1+u1j)*EVdiff + (β2+u2j)*Cond + β3*EVdiff×Cond + uj), where F is cumulative distribution function of standard logistic distribution.
nodes.anchor: we modelled choices with a mixed-effects logistic regression with subject-specific random intercepts

nodes.text: Risk premium calculation: for each participant and condition, fit logistic regression of choice on EVdiff, then define risk premium as the EVdiff value corresponding to 50% risky choices.
nodes.description: Risk premium is defined as the difference between expected value of a lottery and its certainty equivalent; positive values indicate risk aversion.
nodes.anchor: we calculated for each participant a 'risk premium', defined as the difference between the expected value of a lottery and its certainty equivalent

nodes.text: Constant Absolute Risk Aversion (CARA) model estimation: fit exponential utility function U(x,ρ) = 1-e^(-ρx) to choices using probit regression with cumulative Gaussian link function, where ρ represents degree of risk preference.
nodes.description: Certainty equivalent of lottery under CARA is CE = log(1 - ρ*EU)/(-ρ). Fitted using non-linear least-squares in Matlab's nlinfit.m.
nodes.anchor: we used an expected utility theory (EUT) approach to calculate a parameter ρ that describes a decision-maker's risk attitude

nodes.text: Computational modeling of happiness: fit five models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, Responsibility Redux) to Z-scored happiness ratings, each containing terms for certain rewards, expected values, and reward prediction errors with exponential decay over trials (forgetting factor γ).
nodes.description: Models differed in how they represented partner outcomes: Basic had no partner terms; Inequality modeled absolute difference; Guilt-envy separated advantageous and disadvantageous inequality; Responsibility and Responsibility Redux modeled partner reward prediction errors from participant and partner choices separately.
nodes.anchor: we modelled the variations in momentary well-being (happiness ratings) using computational models that considered the influence of recent reward expectations, prediction errors

nodes.text: Parameter recovery for computational models: after fitting each participant's happiness data, synthesize new happiness data using estimated parameters plus 1SD noise, refit model to synthetic data, repeat 10 times, then regress recovered parameters on actual parameters.
nodes.description: This procedure evaluates stability of estimated parameters by testing whether they can be reliably recovered from noisy synthetic data.
nodes.anchor: Stability of the estimated parameters of these models was evaluated by attempting to recover parameters from synthetic data

nodes.text: Linear mixed model regression of happiness on lottery outcomes: regress Z-scored happiness after lottery outcomes in Social and Partner conditions on dummy variables for participant high outcome, partner high outcome, participant decided, and all two-way interactions, with subject-specific random intercepts.
nodes.description: Model equation: Happiness(t) = 1 + β1*sHigh + β2*pHigh + β3*sDec + β4*sHigh*pHigh + β5*sHigh*sDec + β6*pHigh*sDec + uj + εij.
nodes.anchor: we regressed Z-scored momentary happiness ratings reported after these outcomes on dummy variables representing occurrences

nodes.text: fMRI data acquisition: T2*-weighted echo-planar imaging BOLD sequence on 3T Siemens TRIO with 32-channel head coil, TR=2500ms, TE=30ms, 37 slices, 2×2×3mm voxels, flip angle 90°, FOV 192mm, PAT 2 acceleration; plus high-resolution T1-weighted structural image (TR=1660ms, TE=2540ms, 208 slices, 0.8×0.8×0.8mm voxels).
nodes.anchor: Imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens TRIO MRI system

nodes.text: fMRI preprocessing in SPM12: discard first 5 volumes; coregister structural to mean functional; realign functional images to first then mean image using 6-parameter affine transformation; normalize structural to MNI305 template by segmentation and non-linear warping, apply parameters to functionals resampled at 2×2×2mm; smooth with 8mm FWHM Gaussian kernel; high-pass filter at 128s.
nodes.anchor: Data were then pre-processed and analysed as in previous studies using standard procedures in SPM12

nodes.text: First-level fMRI GLM (GLM1): model presentation of choice options, safe choice, risky choice, and receipt of outcomes separately for Social, Partner, and Solo conditions; model high and low lottery outcomes for participant and partner separately for Social and Partner conditions; model happiness rating button presses; convolve all events (modeled as stick functions) with canonical HRF; include 6 motion parameters as regressors of no-interest.
nodes.anchor: The first GLM (GLM1) included the following event types for each session: presentation of choice options, safe choice, risky choice

nodes.text: Model-based fMRI GLM (GLM2): create regressors from Responsibility computational model by fitting model to happiness data, creating stick functions at event times with magnitudes determined by fitted values, convolving with canonical HRF; include regressors for certain rewards (CR), expected values (EV), participant reward prediction errors (sRPE), partner RPE from participant choices (social_pRPE), partner RPE from partner choices (partner_pRPE), happiness button presses, and 6 motion parameters.
nodes.anchor: we created another GLM (GLM2) with regressors designed to identify brain regions whose activation reflected the variables of the best-fitting computational model

nodes.text: Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis using gPPI toolbox: use left insula cluster (from risky>safe outcome contrast) and left STS cluster (from social_pRPE>partner_pRPE contrast) as seeds; create PPI models containing same regressors as GLM1 plus interaction between seed region's first eigenvariate and experimental condition regressors (Safe and Risky choice in Social, Partner, Solo conditions).
nodes.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses

nodes.text: Second-level fMRI analysis: test individual parameter estimate maps in random-effects models including full factorial models for decision phase (factors: Choice [Safe/Risky], Condition [Social/Solo]) and outcome phase (factors: Outcome [Safe/High/Low], Condition [Social/Partner/Solo]); paired t-test contrasting negative lottery outcomes for partner from participant vs. partner choices; model for computational regressors; full factorial models for functional connectivity.
nodes.anchor: Individual parameter estimate maps of the responses to the experimental conditions were assessed in random-effects tests

nodes.text: Linear mixed model analysis of fMRI ROI data: regress parameter estimates from voxels in regions of interest on dummy variables for experimental factors (Choice, Condition, Run, ROI for decision phase; Social, LowOutcome, Run, ROI for outcome phase) with all interactions, using subject-specific random intercepts, fitted with restricted maximum likelihood estimation in Matlab's fitlme.m.
nodes.anchor: we analysed GLM1 parameter estimates from voxels of specific regions of interest using mixed-effects linear regressions

nodes.text: fMRI statistical thresholding: apply family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons at p<0.05 across whole brain or specified volume, based on cluster-forming voxel-wise uncorrected threshold of p<0.001.
nodes.anchor: All clusters reported survive a significance threshold of p < 0.05 with family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons

nodes.text: Comparison with guilt-related brain signature: calculate dot products between individual brain response maps (low partner outcomes from participant vs. partner choices) and the multivariate guilt-related brain signature from Yu et al. 2020; test whether dot products are overall positive using sign test; correlate dot products with behavioral guilt responses using Spearman's correlation.
nodes.anchor: we compared this brain signature to the neural responses obtained in our task (response to low partner outcomes resulting from participant vs. partner responses)

nodes.text: This paper: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions
nodes.description: The current study investigating neural mechanisms of interpersonal guilt and responsibility during risky social decisions.
nodes.anchor: This study investigated the neural mechanisms involved in feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility

nodes.text: Rutledge et al. 2014: A computational and neural model of momentary subjective well-being
nodes.description: Previous study that developed computational models of how risky choices and their outcomes influence momentary happiness, which the current study builds upon.
nodes.anchor: inspired by findings from experimental social decision-making tasks

nodes.text: Rutledge et al. 2016: Association of neural and emotional impacts of reward prediction errors with major depression
nodes.description: Previous study that extended computational modeling of happiness to social contexts, including inequality between self and other outcomes.
nodes.anchor: This allowed us to fit computational models to happiness data

nodes.text: Edelson et al. 2018: Neural mechanisms of responsibility aversion
nodes.description: Landmark study reporting mechanisms involved in seeking or avoiding responsibility in decisions affecting a group, finding involvement of medial prefrontal cortex, anterior insula, and temporo-parietal junction.
nodes.anchor: One landmark study reported on the mechanisms involved in seeking or avoiding responsibility in decisions affecting a group of individuals

nodes.text: Yu et al. 2020: Multivariate neural signature for guilt
nodes.description: Study that re-analyzed two previous neuroimaging studies of guilt and obtained a multivariate guilt-related brain signature (GRBS), which the current study used for comparison.
nodes.anchor: A recent study by Yu and colleagues re-analysed the results of two previous neuroimaging studies of guilt and obtained a neural multivariate guilt-related brain signature

nodes.text: Bastin et al. 2016: Brain regions associated with guilt
nodes.description: Study associating anterior insula, dorsal cingulate cortex, and left temporo-parietal junction with feelings of guilt.
nodes.anchor: Several brain regions have been associated with the feeling of guilt: the anterior insula (aIns)

nodes.text: Koban et al. 2013: Neural correlates of guilt in perception-pain task
nodes.description: Study where partners received painful stimuli when participants made errors during a difficult perception task, evoking activations in left anterior insula and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
nodes.anchor: In another study, partners received painful stimuli when participants made errors during a difficult perception task

nodes.text: The guilt effect observed in behavior is driven by empathy for the partner's negative outcome rather than interpersonal guilt.
nodes.description: Alternative explanation for the happiness decrease following low partner outcomes when participants chose: the effect could reflect empathy rather than guilt specifically. The authors acknowledge this possibility but interpret their findings as guilt based on the operational definition.
nodes.anchor: we cannot ascertain whether people experienced guilt, shame, regret, disappointment or another specific emotion during the experiment

nodes.text: The anterior insula activation reflects general negative emotion or empathy rather than guilt specifically.
nodes.description: Alternative account of the left anterior insula finding: this region is associated with multiple negative emotions and empathy, not uniquely with guilt. The authors acknowledge this but argue the pattern fits guilt based on their operational definition and similarity to published guilt signatures.
nodes.anchor: The aIns region has also been associated with empathy for negative emotions such as disgust or pain

nodes.text: Participants' choices in the Social condition were influenced by strategic considerations about the partner's expectations rather than by risk preferences.
nodes.description: Alternative explanation for choice behavior: differences between Social and Solo conditions could reflect strategic thinking about what the partner expects rather than changes in risk preference. The paper tests this by comparing risk preferences across conditions.
nodes.anchor: participants chose the risky option more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition

nodes.text: The happiness decrease when participants chose reflects general responsibility aversion or decision-making burden rather than guilt about outcomes.
nodes.description: Alternative explanation for lower happiness when participants made choices: this could reflect the psychological cost of responsibility itself rather than guilt about specific outcomes. The authors note this possibility, citing Edelson et al.'s responsibility aversion findings.
nodes.anchor: being assigned the role of the decider in a social setting may make people slightly unhappy, perhaps due to 'weight of the responsibility'

nodes.text: The partner's decisions were made by an algorithm rather than a real person, which may have reduced the emotional impact and validity of the social manipulation.
nodes.description: Limitation the authors acknowledge: using an algorithm instead of real partner choices could have weakened emotional responses. They argue their findings remain valid because partner outcomes still influenced happiness, but cannot exclude this alternative.
nodes.anchor: The partner's decisions were in fact taken by an algorithm. This was not communicated to the participants

nodes.text: In both studies, risk premiums did not differ significantly between Solo and Social conditions (Study 1: t(39) = 1.53, p = 0.134, d = 0.24, BF10 = 0.49; Study 2: t(43) = -0.21, p = 0.84, d = -0.03, BF10 = 0.17).
nodes.description: Null result showing that a simpler, more robust measure of risk aversion showed no difference between conditions, arguing against the alternative that strategic considerations drove choice differences.
nodes.anchor: Risk premiums did not differ between Social and Solo conditions

nodes.text: Responsibility for positive lottery outcomes for the partner did not influence happiness (both studies, all |t| < 1.3, p > 0.2, BF10 < 0.2).
nodes.description: Null result showing that the guilt effect was specific to negative outcomes, not a general effect of responsibility, supporting the guilt interpretation over general responsibility aversion.
nodes.anchor: Responsibility for choices did not influence happiness following positive lottery outcomes for the partner

nodes.text: Participant happiness correlated with partner rewards obtained in the current trial (Study 1: F(1,2426) = 128.6, p < 0.001, R² = 0.05; Study 2: F(1,1735) = 111.8, p < 0.001, R² = 0.06).
nodes.description: Evidence that participants were emotionally engaged with partner outcomes despite the partner being simulated by an algorithm, arguing against the alternative that the deception invalidated the social manipulation.
nodes.anchor: participant momentary happiness correlated with rewards obtained in the current trial by the participant and by the partner

second_pass.notes: Found five alternatives: two competing interpretations of the main findings (empathy vs guilt for behavior and insula activation), one about choice behavior (strategic vs risk preference), one about general responsibility effects, and one methodological limitation (algorithm partner). The paper argues against the first three with specific evidence but leaves the last two partially open as acknowledged limitations. Added support edges for manipulation checks (e11 to c6, ae1 to c6, ae2 to c1) that were previously unconnected.
